utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. This is June 21st, 2007. Last day of the hearing for this witness. I would like first to welcome our witness and representatives from the Prosecution, counsel for Defence, as well as the accused. I note that Mr. Coric is still away, and I wish him well and hope he comes back soon. Furthermore, I must read a short oral decision regarding the extension of a deadline. On June 14th, 2007, the Chamber was seized of a motion by the Prosecution requesting an extension of deadline to file its seven-day answer after the filing of the new motion from Prlic's Defence requiring the case to be disjoined. Accused Prlic filed his new motion on June 19, 2007. The Chamber, according to Rule 126 bis, is granting the motion and gives the Prosecution seven days as of 19 June 2007, i.e., up until June 26, 2007, to file the request. So the Prosecution will have seven days to file the answer, following the request of Prlic's motion requesting a severance of his own case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, regarding the time allotted, according to the registrar's calculations, 3D still has one hour, 4D has 35 minutes, and 6D, 30 minutes. Of course, you can split the time as you wish among each other. While we're at it, to make sure that we don't forget it, next week we will have a witness scheduled for the entire week. It's a witness coming from the European Mission. The Prosecution has been allotted six hours, and the Defence will have eight hours, unless counsel change the time -- split the time among each other. But the Chamber believes that Mr. Pusic should have one hour and 40 minutes; Mr. Prlic should have one hour and 40 minutes; Mr. Stojic, one hour and 40 minutes; Mr. Petkovic, one hour and 40 minutes; and the two other accused will each get 40 minutes. The time was split in this manner because Messrs. Pusic, Prlic, Petkovic, and Coric met the witness, which was not the case for the two others, because the four -- the four ones at first had met the witness during meetings and the others hadn't. But, of course, you can split the time as you want, and maybe Prosecution will not use its six hours since many exhibits have already been shown to another witness. Now we'll continue with the hearing, and I will give the floor to Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all in the courtroom. Your Honours, I see that in terms of this time calculation our Defence has 35 minutes left. I would just like to draw your attention to the fact that, in agreement with my colleague Mr. Karnavas, I ceded about 10 minutes of my time to the Prlic Defence because I gave General Praljak's Defence about 20 or 25 minutes. That's what I promised them, so that I would have half an hour left. I know that Mr. Karnavas used more than these 10-odd minutes that I ceded to him, but I thought that we have a relatively long day today in terms of the six hours for cross-examination, so I would like, therefore, my time to be corrected, and could you please record it as 50 minutes rather than 30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, the Bench is a bit surprised. We thought that the time you had given to Mr. Karnavas was going to be subtracted from the time allotted to you. And since you also ceded time to Mr. Praljak, there we are. According to our calculations, you only have 35 minutes left. I believe that you will take the floor last, and if we have time left, of course we will grant you additional time. We'll first start with the others, and if we have time left, you will get it. But as you know, the allotment of time is extremely complicated. Personally, I'd rather that you settled the matter amongst yourselves, among counsel, and that we wouldn't have to intervene. Unfortunately, we have to intervene in order to settle problems, but it's difficult. I believe that Mr. Praljak's Defence is up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam. I would kindly ask you, due to the fact that our time is short, that we simply go through some documents, and could you just briefly reply whether you do know about something or do not, as you've been doing until now. As I worked in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, as I was involved in political activity there, we had to deal with the question of refugees often. I don't know if you know that the Croatian army very often made available some of their own facilities, hotels, in the area of Gasinci. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent to which the media reported on it at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you also know that since the Croatian army was expeditious then, do you know that Adalbert Rebic often asked us to put people up quickly, to intervene from the point of view of construction, building, and so on? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You don't know about that. Could you please look at this binder that you have here and could we go through education in the Republic of Croatia first given to refugees.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D 001096.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. I haven't. What's the last digit? The last number I have here is 921. I haven't got 96. Oh, sorry, I do have it -- no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The third one from the end.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third one from the end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, 3D 0136. I have misread it.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it open.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: "Extraterritorial Schooling of Pupils from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia." I have 67 documents, of course not all of them are here now. Could you please look at page -- the next page, 571. That is the graph that pertains to those schools.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: According to the information that I have and that is contained here, the Croatian government or, rather, the Ministry of Education established 36 schools attached to their own that had additional training in the Bosnian language. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Oh, you don't. Do you know that the Republic of Croatia, without any major problems whatsoever, allowed enrollment in the regular schools of the Republic of Croatia all refugees, including Bosniak Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, would you look at 572. 572.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any numbers of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just skip a page. 3D 26-0572. That's what the page number is.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That is the government of the Republic of Croatia. Mrs. Girardi Jurkic is the signatory. Did you know that at the time she was the Minister of Education of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Praljak's microphone please be adjusted. Thank you. We cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, the interpreters have difficulties hearing you and ask to adjust the microphone. Maybe you test if it is good for them. If you speak, one, two, three, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is it good with interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you hear me now. Now I'm going to speak a bit louder and then people will be able to hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says here that the Republic of Croatia is paying for all the education costs, teaching, teachers, just like for pupils from Croatia. We have figures here as well. So in those school years, there were 32.000 pupils, refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, out of which 25.000 in elementary schools and almost 7.000 in secondary schools; and in pre-school institutions, there were 2.800 children from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Madam, were you aware of these figures?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Can we please go on now. Please look at the next document, 574 is the page. Again, the government of the Republic of Croatia, the Ministry of Education, Schools and Sport. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. 573 is what I have, and then after that 603.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How is that possible? Please a have a look.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 574. We'll try to cut things short. Again, in paragraph 3, again compulsory education for children of all age groups, appropriate curricula in the Republic of Croatia. In the third paragraph it says: "In agreement with the vice-president, Dr. Mate Granic, it's been agreed that a preliminary list of expenses should be made related to the cost of documentation of 70.000 children because these expenses cannot be settled by means for the school system provided by the state budget." And then it says here: "84 million Croatian dinars per month, whereas for the manuals, an additional 116 million HRD should be provided." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you know that the Republic of Croatia or, rather, the Ministry of Culture and Sport, that is to say, the government of Croatia, gave textbooks free of charge to all students enrolled in schools of the Republic of Croatia, regardless of whether they were refugees or not refugees? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that all the payments came from the budget or, rather, from extra budgetary resources, and that all of this was paid for by the Republic of Croatia? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let us go back to something else. Yesterday you said that you gave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Praljak. While we're at it, on the next page, it also says that there will be a request for help from the international community as well, so perhaps it's not everything that would be paid by Croatia. Or how do I have to understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Assistance was rendered by the international community, no doubt about that. However, the subject that we are dealing with in the time that is available for looking at the finances allocated by the Republic of Croatia for different types of aid and assistance, that would have yielded at least five or six or seven more -- times more results in terms of the financial burden of the Republic of Croatia than what we heard yesterday, the 800 million or whatever, rather, 1 billion dollars that was referred to. That merits a special debate. However, for schooling there is no information that anything was received because that was not considered to be the kind of form of humanitarian assistance that food and medicine would fall under.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, can we say, therefore, that the educational system of the Republic of Croatia, to the best your knowledge, fully, without any discrimination whatsoever, with full intensity, organised and paid irrespective of whether pupils came from Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether they were Croats or Muslims or whoever, whether they were Croats from the Republic of Croatia? Was there any discrimination whatsoever? There was no discrimination. And do you have any example that would refute that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of some of examples. I do have some examples.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court whether it was one example, two examples, where these examples took place? Did you contact Mr. Rebic or Girardi Jurkic and tell them that the director of a school made a mistake anywhere? Was there a name and surname? In what school? In what place? ?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I handed over all my documents, so I can't tell you off the top of my head, so I can't quote a document or a date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Who did you hand over your documents over to?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Bisera Turkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you remember how many examples you could have quoted there? Because they are, after all, examples which would have stuck in your mind.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never liked to rely on my memory, because I might have gained the impression, the subjective impression, that there were a lot, whereas it might not correspond to the facts. So that wouldn't be fair on my part. I wouldn't be doing an honest job.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, we're looking for the truth here, so any fact that can contribute to that I would find acceptable. Now, according to your knowledge or the present documents that we're looking at, were there a lot of exceptions or is that how Croatia reacted?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the academic year of 1992 and 1993, I don't remember any such problems existing. But as I can tell you, there were a lot of calls, ringing up the embassy, asking that children be enrolled in regular schools.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. So we don't know what the quantity of this was. Now, if we go on to the next document, which is on page 569, the 4th of February, 1993, that school year, you're talking about academic year of 1992-1993, take a look at this document. It says, "We are sending you the school curriculum ..." It's just the following document. Just go on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I think I made a mistake. 595 is the document number.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And it says, "We are sending you the school curriculum according to which the self-organised primary schools in Croatia, working for refugees from the RBiH." Do you know, madam -- or, rather, did you try and organise some schools yourself or, rather, you embassy? Is that true, that you tried to organise some schools yourself?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. No. According to my information, an attempt was made, but the job was given up after three months, and a reduced curriculum from 1993, which is on page 597, says that -- this reduced curriculum says that the Bosnian language will be taught, that that will be a subject, for five lessons a week for class 1. Is that what it says at the top, as a heading, "Reduced Curriculum," et cetera? And the number is 597 of the page. Page 597.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this page I can see that it says, "Subject: Bosnian Language, Class 1."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's right. And then it goes on to say, "Five lessons per week." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did an official language called the Bosnian language exist, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. You don't know. Well, not to belabour the point, I'm now going to read out on the next page for class 2 -- or, rather, for class 3 the same things. "Subject: Bosnian Language, Class 3, five lessons a week." Then class 5 has three lessons a week. Can you see all that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the following page. Yes, "Reduced Curriculum," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now let's look at class 5. I'll go through that quickly. It says, "Tone Seliskar." Do you agree that that would be a Slovene?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went to school a long time ago. I really can't say whether he's a writer. He is a Slovenian, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then we have Andersen's Tales, Hans Christian Andersen. Then we have Branko Copic. Do you know that Branko Copic is a Serb writer, in fact?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, he's a very well-known children's writer from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serb by ethnicity, Branko Copic. Have you ever heard of the next name, Musika Kapacic [phoen]? Then we --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then we have another Muslim Bosniak writer, five or six lines from the bottom. Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In lines 7 and 8, I can't see it yet. But yes, I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's move on to page 8. Three lessons a week. You see Izet Sarajlic, a Bosniak poet. After Jure Kastelan, we come to these poets, Ivan Slamukic [phoen], Jure Sarajlic. Izet Sarajlic, is he a Bosniak Muslim poet?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he's a poet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Then below that, four or five lines down, we have Savfet-beg Basagic. Have you heard of that poet, a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then we have five or six lines further on a selection from Bosnian-Herzegovinian poetry. Then we have Copic again, Branko Copic. Then we have Meso Selimovic, another Muslim Bosniak; and then Hasan Kikic and Dervis Susic. Then we have Dizdarevic and so on and so forth. And then we have the death of Hasanaginica, or, rather, Hasanaginica. So are all these Bosniak Muslims, Hasan Kikic, Meso Selimovic, Dizdarevic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. But to the best of my knowledge I think that all the names you've mentioned are Bosnian-Herzegovinian, of BH origin, including Mr. Copic, to the best of my recollections, was a Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to test you on your education, but can we see from this that there was no national or ethnic discrimination in the subjects taught in Croatian schools, the fact that the children were Bosniak Muslims, from a curriculum like this? Is that obvious?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but this is signed by Mr. Lejla -- Mrs. Lejla Aksamija. She was a refugee. And it was only in cooperation with the rest of the refugees that the refugees organised schools during this period of time according to this curriculum that she sent out to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But did the educational ministry of Croatia implement this curriculum that was compiled by a Bosniak lady? Do you know about that? That in the schools in the Republic of Croatia, the curriculum devised and written by your friend and collaborator, who was a Bosniak and provided this curriculum, did the Croatian authorities okay this and have the programme taught in the schools?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that explicitly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How about implicitly? Do you know of the opposite stand?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I think it is only fair from the Bench to draw your attention to the fact that this, of course, is a paper with a programme. It does not prove that any of this was actually taught in any school. I just want to draw your attention to this. Also, we have had no translation, so it was rather difficult for us to follow the last part of the interrogation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, I said at the beginning on page 595 that this was a curriculum sent out, and the curriculum was adopted. It was put forward and adopted. And on 596, page 596, it says that the ministry approved the programme. Apart from that, Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, I don't have to prove this. It's not up to me to prove it. I know about it. I was included in it. I know for a fact that the programme was implemented and that all children could enroll. I'm not going to speak about some exceptions in a school where some principal or headmaster didn't want to, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, that you don't have to prove anything here, but now you have become a witness and that I think is not what the cross-examination is meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I have not become a witness. The witness herself dealt with refugees. The refugees included children and those children went to Croatian schools. And not dozens of children but 40.000 children in the pre-school institutions and so on, as she ought to me. I understand that the lady had a lot of work to do and there were just six or seven people to do all of that job. And there were thousands of refugees, so she was overloaded. But I've just brought in the documents here and I'm asking the lady whether she knows. If Mrs. Krajsek says she doesn't know, then well and good. But I asked her whether there was any discrimination and she will tell me whether she knew about that or not. I'm going to ask her.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you know about that, madam, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before that, I'm going --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please. Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning. Judge Trechsel, I couldn't agree with you more. I mean, in the last few minutes, we've had continuing examples of Mr. Praljak acting as a witness and making absolute assertions as if they are true, as if they are evidence. Now, of course, if the time comes and Mr. Praljak would like to take the witness stand under oath and give evidence, that's his prerogative. But it's not his prerogative to stand up and just simply tell the Court facts. "I'm telling you this because I know it to be true," and we've heard a number of instances of that in the last few minutes. However, at the same time, the Prosecution is happy to receive whatever information Mr. Praljak would like to provide to us and to the Chamber, and collects that information on a regular basis so that at the end of the case, of course, we can tell the Chamber what Mr. Praljak has admitted and what he agrees to as to the facts in the case. Having said that, Your Honour, could I just ask for clarification. There was just an assertion by Mr. Praljak that one of the documents we had looked to, other than Mr. Praljak himself, but that he had put a document in evidence which confirms that this programme was in fact adopted and put in place in the Croatian schools. I have to say I'm having a very difficult time following the documents this morning the way they're organised. Can I please ask and can Mr. Praljak please tell us exactly which of the documents he's addressed this morning that he says confirms that this programme -- the proposal by a Bosnian refugee, not the Croatian government, but the proposal by a Bosnian woman refugee, which document shows that that was, in fact, accepted and put in place in the schools? If he could please point us to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, can you please give us this clarification regarding this particular document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The programme for schools in the Republic of Croatia existed. Now, in this document, on page 574, you can see how much money was set aside, what those figures are. And in document 595, quite obviously Mrs. Lejla was asked to devise an additional programme for the Bosnian language. Now, in my file relating to education, I have a total of 67 documents here. Your Honours, it is quite impossible to get through all those 67 documents here with the witness. I would be happy if we were able to do that, but obviously these proceedings are such that that is impossible. So I put the document to the witness, I showed her the document that Ms. Lejla sent out, her programme.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Interpreters, sorry. Thank you. I just would like to thank Mr. Praljak for answering the question that I had invited through the Chamber, and the record now stands clarified. He has not pointed to any document showing that the proposal was, in fact, accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we're really wasting time here. It's up to you to evaluate the documents. Mr. Praljak quite clearly said that we can conclude that the Ministry of Education, that is to say, the responsible ministry, asked for a curriculum from the special or separate schools that organised themselves, because by law the Ministry of Education, by law, had to approve the curricula for every school, even foreign schools. We had schools, for example, for foreign diplomats' children. So every teaching programme, whether it be in France, in Croatia, in Bulgaria, an extraterritorial programme must be approved by the Ministry of Education of the host country. Now, this page on the document 595 was sent out, the document by Mrs. Lejla, it was sent out to the government of the Republic of Croatia, the Ministry for Culture and Education. So the ministry took note of this. It was sent to the ministry. It is reasonable to conclude that the ministry asked for this programme; otherwise, it would be illogical. Of course, in the Defence case we can bring in an official from the Ministry of Culture and Education who will tell you, Yes, we received it; we didn't act adversely; we approved it or not or we did such and such. We can bring in a witness to that effect. But this is quite a logical sequence of events, what we're discussing here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The Chamber will be absolutely able to evaluate documentation for what it is worth, and I think Mr. Praljak should continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but to respond.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely what I was saying. It is up to the Chamber, and the Prosecution wishes to launch an argument. That's precisely what I said. It's up to the Trial Chamber to decide what weight to give to the document, in view of the fact that it was, indeed, sent to the Ministry of Culture and Education and in view of the standards in every civilised country in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, sorry, but I am not launching into an argument. I'm making an objection, which is my duty and responsibility to do when I think it appropriate. But with respect to my good friend Mr. Kovacic, not only Mr. Praljak is now acting as a witness but now Mr. Kovacic is acting as a witness, explaining the Croatian school system and making assertions about what it did or did not do. And if we could just please -- I fully agree with Judge Trechsel. If we could just please put questions to the witness and ask her instead of making assertions, Mr. Praljak simply making assertions, and put questions to the witness, we could move much more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may briefly assist the Trial Chamber. The objection that you raised, Judge Trechsel, or the observation that you made I think caused some confusion only because of the way, perhaps, it was stated. Obviously, it was an observation that we all, as lawyers, are mindful of, and that is when we pose a question, especially on cross-examination, to a witness because it appears as if we, the lawyers, are testifying through the question, that it's assumed that we have a good-faith basis for putting forward the proposition that's in the question itself. I think what you were trying to alert to Mr. Praljak was that he should have a good-faith basis for the assertions that he's making. And what I heard from Mr. Kovacic is that in due time they will demonstrate that everything that Mr. Praljak is saying, they have a good-faith basis. But cross-examination, the art of it, the science of it, is where the lawyer is, in essence, providing the answer and the witness usually saying yes or no and then maybe explaining, but there is a good-faith basis. So when Mr. Scott objected, Mr. Kovacic demonstrated the good-faith basis that they have. At some point, of course, they're going to have to prove it, they're going to have to provide some proof. And if they don't provide any proof, then obviously that question has no value at all and you will consider that in your ultimate evaluation of the evidence. That's how I understand the process. So I understood exactly what you were trying to convey, which was merely a cautionary instruction to Mr. Praljak that anything that he puts to the witness, it has to have a good-faith basis. I think that was the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am sure, Mr. Karnavas, that you understood what I was aiming at, and I'm also sure that when you said, They have to prove it, you were looking at Mr. Praljak but you were thinking of the Prosecutor, because the Defence does not have to prove anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They don't have to prove any -- they don't have to prove any assertions that they're making. You can choose not to -- not to accept them. But if, for instance, there was an objection early on, and I believe -- I believe it was you, Judge Trechsel, with respect to one -- one remark that -- or one question that was posed by Mr. Praljak, if we look at paragraph 24 of the statement, the statement that you have admitted. You have admitted. You've accepted. It says here that Croatia never financed or co-financed -- co-financed these costs which can be proved through documentation. Now Mr. Praljak is proving the opposite and he gets cautioned because it says here they co-financed. He never said that they exclusively financed, so he's doing exactly what any good lawyer would be doing. So I don't see what the problem is. And the Prosecutor can object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could we then go on, Mr. Karnavas. If you don't see where the problem is, I think you shouldn't go on speaking. Mr. Praljak, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, you may proceed, but as the Presiding Judge here, I'd like to say something now. The Defence is entitled to show a number of documents to the witness. That's what the Defence is currently doing. These documents, on the face of it, seem official, because if we look at document 595, we see that there is a stamp, and this document looks like an administrative document produced by the Ministry for Culture and Education. In this document, we see that there is a mention of various programmes, various curricula. Bosnian authors are to be studied as part of this curricula. That is what we read here. There is also reference made to foreign authors, and Franck and Romeo and Juliet is also mentioned here. So here we have a very official looking curriculum. The Defence then asks the witness whether she knows that the 170.000 children coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina were taught according to this curriculum. The witness answered no. Now, if the Prosecution decides to challenge this, they can do it as part of the re-examination. They can produce documents challenging this. So please proceed, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to correct the record. It is not up to me to challenge evidence that has not been admitted, and counsel -- Mr. Praljak asserting something is not evidence, nor is there any foundation for the documentation. So it is not for me to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't play on words, Mr. Scott. Mr. Praljak will request the admission of these documents, and if you challenge these documents, you will be entitled to do it, because we should not forget that this is part and parcel of your demonstration about the JCE. So the Defence is perfectly entitled to challenge your case and it's trying to do it through these documents. Mr. Praljak, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, you, as a person who was officially dealing with refugees, you or any one of the officials working with you, did you check the authenticity and truthfulness of what we read out just now?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm so confused now. Are we talking about the curriculum in the regular schools of the Republic of Croatia or about the curriculum for extraterritorial schools of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, let's take things one at a time.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Apart from isolated examples, as you had put it, can you indicate any kind of discriminatory attitude taken by the Ministry of Education of the Republic of Croatia towards refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to Croatian children, speaking in global terms, in general terms, Croatian children from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I do beg your pardon. Could you repeat your question. I'm not too --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, did you notice that the Croatian government, the Croatian state, the Croatian authorities, were treating refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina differently, regardless of their ethnic background, in relation to the children born in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you give us examples?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell us where and when.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, that is to say, the school year of 1993-1994, the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia had an insurmountable problem in terms of enrolling in the regular schools of the Republic of Croatia because they could not bring in the documents that were required by law.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: What documentation? Can you tell the Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inter alia birth certificate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's resolve the question of birth certificate, madam. How many people in Croatia had birth certificates from churches? How many communists were there who never christened their children in churches?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Oh, come on, you don't know? Were there 300 communists in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were there 300.000 communists in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you say a christening birth certificate, does that mean that that is simply someone who has a document that he was born somewhere?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So what do you mean when you say "birth certificate," that somebody was christened in a church?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were given interpretation in schools, what it meant, "birth certificate," a christening birth certificate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They simply didn't have that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look, I'm going to show you another document later where it says this. But, first of all, in the Republic of Croatia, if you look at all towns from Bosnia-Herzegovina, weren't clubs, local clubs of Doboze, Camaglia, et cetera, founded?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that different clubs were established.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: These clubs, did the state, that is to say, the Republic of Croatia, recognise these clubs as being a replacement for the municipal authorities for the municipalities from where they were expelled?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know. But I'm going to show you a document later on. Now I'm going to ask you the following: You said in your statement that in order to have your refugee papers extended, you had to go to the municipality where you had fled from, so on and so forth. I'm going to show you another Rebic document stating that it was sufficient to go to the club that was established by the refugees and to give a certificate that this person was a refugee. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not a single refugee came to see me with that kind of document, that kind of document from Adalbert Rebic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. You don't know, and what can I do about that. All right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D 01033. No, sorry, I have misspoken. 3D 01034. 01034.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: This says, "Care for wounded and ill members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and civilians in Croatian hospitals from 1992 to 1995." You see in the binders prepared for this trial there are 1.232 documents that pertain to this, and of course we can't go through all of that, but I would like to ask you the following: Please open page 441. We have already put this to the Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That 3.991 Bosniak Muslims, for the most part wounded persons, seriously ill persons, through the HZ HB in 1993 and partly in 1994 were treated in the KBC Split hospital at three different localities. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this is a correct piece of information, but I cannot discuss the matter. I know that many of them were treated, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you tell me the following: Did you visit wounded persons in hospitals?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Split on one occasion and in Toplice. I cannot remember exactly -- well, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Toplice near Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me the following: To the best of your knowledge, you, from the embassy, or any other authority of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you ever pay anything for medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that in addition to hospitalisation, that is to say, treatment in hospitals of serious cases, that there were general rights among the refugees to be treated in medical institutions of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to primary health care?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of primary health care, that it was accessible to refugees.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Equally, like to all other citizens of the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was accessible to refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina without any additional comments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. That will do. Tell me, what about basic dental health care, regardless of prosthetics and so on?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's part of primary care, I assume that that was accessible, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now please open page 443.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The same document.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please take a look. Dr. Tamin Akram is seeking the following, and he was issued medicaments, according to a specification, by Ms. Zupanovic, who was a head nurse for medicaments, and this was done at the request primarily of doctors who were Bosniak Muslims, medicines were issued. Do you know who Dr. Tamin Akram is?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you hear of Mrs. Zupanovic, who was a legend down there in terms of receiving and treating the wounded and so on?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name rings a bell, but -- well, it rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, let's look at page 444.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says, "At the request of the children's embassy from Sarajevo, according to Dr. Hozo's recommendations and approval by MS Dr. G. Dodik for the needs of DZ Breza." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document. For the needs of Banovic municipality, at the request of Merhamet, again medicines being provided. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, do you know Zupanovic and do you know who Dragica Sabatos is, who took these things down there?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now look at document 453.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 453?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, page 453. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Dr. Sulejman Sulic, is he a Bosnian Muslim, judging by his name?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by his name, he can be a Muslim, he can being a Bosniak, he can be a Bosniak Muslim, I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Again, he's looking for medicaments. Can you see is that? It's the same document.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read the document? Should I read it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, there is no need. These are documents --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now let us look at page 477.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The number of wounded persons and civilians, mostly Muslims according to ethnicity, in some hospitals of the Republic of Croatia. Split Firule; Split Krizine; Split Toplice, Zagreb; 2.982. Karlovac, Slavonski Brod, 2.730; Vinkovci. Of course this does not include all the hospitals because I was collecting data on a private basis. But at any rate the total is 10.623. Can you confirm or challenge the assertion that the majority of these 10.000 or so were Bosniak Muslims who were treated in the mentioned hospital here?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You never kept any records or anything?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't work on that. This was not my line of work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did anyone keep records of this kind in your embassy?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a medical department that dealt with this particular subject matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Further on, do you know from the money that you received - and we will see how you did get your money - did you participate in any way in the medical treatment of all these persons of Bosnian Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I just know about part of the financial resources that I personally gave to wounded persons when I visited them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The wounded but not hospitals.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, no, I wasn't really involved in that. It wasn't my line of work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So we will agree -- but, anyway, this is my question: It's not only you from the embassy but also other people from the embassy, and especially people who were working on behalf of the Islamic Republic of Iran in Zagreb, did you take money to Bosniak Muslims in hospitals and did you give them money, money into their hands?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about myself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you did that, too?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not the way that you are interpreting that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At any rate you gave them money, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I gave money to wounded Croats who were lying in hospital beds right next to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. I'm not saying anything --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they also signed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's exactly what I wanted to say. You are overlapping, you're speaking too fast, and the interpreters cannot follow so it doesn't reach the Chamber. So please do not speak too quickly. And after finishing, after the other has finished, give a pause for the interpreters to translate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel. What is killing me is the sight of that clock over there and that is the explanation for this bit of nervousness on my part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 489.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you recognise Mr. Izetbegovic's signature?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So look at this document. Do you know that Mr. Ejub Ganic had a traffic accident and that he was treated in Croatia at the clinical hospital in Split?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from the Croatian media.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic is thanking everyone there and giving his -- paying his respects and expressing his gratitude and saying that this should not be forgotten.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot read this document. It is illegible and my spectacles do not match this font.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. I am going to read it. "As many times so far, your expertise in which you are entirely devoted to your occupation of physician resulted when we needed it the most. This shall never be forgotten here." "This will not be forgotten here." Yes. You knew of the event, did you?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you know Mrs. Izetbegovic throughout the war was in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: As a refugee. You didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the wife of Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. You didn't know that. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on from hospitals and take a look at document 3D 01029. It's at the beginning, the second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Praljak give the page number as well, please, thank you, because we don't have the document numbered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have found it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, if you look at page 82.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that on the territory of the Republic of Croatia during the war that we're discussing here, 234 humanitarian organisations were registered?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact number. That there were a lot of them, that I do know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, if you look at pages 87 onwards, 87 and 88, then for each of these organisations you will find their names, the telephone numbers, fax numbers, addresses, and so on. But anyway, you said you knew that there were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were there quite a number from the Islamic countries, from the Islamic world?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, could you take a look at page 121, please. Page 121.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't find that number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It is page 121 of that same document or binder, and just turn the pages until you get to page 121. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I'm afraid I can't seem to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, it's two pages in front of that last document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: If you turn back two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If the usher could assist, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give me the page number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 121.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two pages before the next yellow sticker, 1030.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But that's not the same, that page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, maybe you don't have enough time, but what would be good is to give us the page number in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D 260121.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The numbers are different here. I have the document but not with that number. I think I've found the document you wish me to look at.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. It's a request to the Main Staff of the HVO dated the 9th of June, 1993. The BH army, Mr. Siber. Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And he is requesting that the wounded from Tuzla and Split be taken in. Did you know that there were regular helicopter flights to transport the wounded from Tuzla and other parts of BH to Zagreb hospitals?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know whether they were regular flights. I knew of some flights, and I was present on one occasion when the wounded, a group of wounded, arrived from Tuzla to Split.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now turn to page 113 next, please, 113.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that before this document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It is the 19th of April, 1994, signed by Ms. Bisera Turkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19th of April, yes. It says, "For Bisera Turkovic."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: She says, "Once again, we would like to express our gratitude," et cetera, et cetera, and then she says information about the following: "Bosnia and Herzegovinian citizens who, with the help of the UNHCR, arriving at the border of the Republic of Croatia, with the aim of going on to third countries." This talks about the fact that the UNHCR was the institution which was the main organiser among the Muslims primarily but also Croatian refugees from BH in transporting these people to third countries. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that it was the principal organisation, but I did know that it helped those who wanted to leave for third countries. That I do know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But Ms. Bisera Turkovic says, "We appreciate and accept the offered cooperation between the Office for Expelled Persons and Refugees and the Embassy by which the control of work organisations would be introduced dealing with forwarding civilians from Bosnia-Herzegovina." Is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says what you've just read out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And at the bottom it says, "We're sending you a copy of the letter sent to the UNHCR by way of information about certain UNHCR activities on the territory of the Republic of Croatia," and we'll go back to that document in just a moment. Is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you know that the UNHCR dealt with matters of this kind, but you don't know what its organisational structure was; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the volume, how much work of this kind it engaged in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In view of the large number of institutions dealing with humanitarian aid, do you happen to know that there were all sorts there, if I can put it that way, all sorts of things were going on, various clandestine trafficking. There was mirky business, there were spies, there was black marketeering, et cetera. Do you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you agree with me when I say that this introduced -- or, rather, had very serious consequences and was detrimental to the organisations that worked well, did good work; that there were a lot of problems because it cast a shadow on all of them?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And do you know that some of these organisations wanted to introduce large quantities of medicines with a shelf-life date that had already expired and they wanted to bring them into both BH and Croatia. Now look at page 119, please.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where to look for these numbers that you're quoting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's straight out of the document we've just been discussing.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, the signatory there is Mr. Sefko Omerbasic on behalf of the Mesihat organisation; and on behalf of Merhamet, Mr. Aganovic; and Mrs. Andzelita Jokic on behalf of the Croatian Caritas organisation. Now, do you know Mr. Omerbasic and Dr. Aganovic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In that proclamation dated the 16th of September -- yes, I'm being asked to slow down. I'll do my best. Yes, the 16th of September, 1993, they say that they want publicly to state that the Croatian Caritas and Merhamet and Mesihat are cooperating in various ways, despite those who keep denying the existence of this cooperation. Now, do you know who it was who endeavoured to introduce this rift between the organisations and among the organisations, this discord between the Caritas, Merhamet and Mesihat? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At the end it says, "We would like to reiterate our serious concern in view of this which makes life more difficult with these secret" -- it says "secret things that make this Holocaust difficult, which includes the innocent. Once again, we sincerely invite all those whom this may concern to consider the detrimental consequences of such actions." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Sefko Omerbasic and Dr. Izet Aganovic, were they prominent Muslims in Croatia, intellectuals and so on?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of them were highly respected, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. Now, can you tell Their Honours what the reason would be for their writing this proclamation and what secret operations or secret actions to introduce unrest and to introduce black marketeering and so on that they were referring to?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to ask you to take a look at another document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene, I apologise, because quite obviously because of the overlapping and speed, an important statement made by the witness was not recorded. The witness clearly confirmed that Dr. Sefko Omerbasic and Dr. Aganovic were indeed prominent, I think she said renowned, members of the Muslim religious community in Zagreb. We don't have that in the record, quite obviously because the speakers were overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, that's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, will the witness then confirm her answer and tell us what she said when asked about the stature of these two individuals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I know that both of these two individuals were highly respected in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's sufficient. But they were Muslims, were they not?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Now let's look at document 3D 01045. "45" are the last two digits, madam. Before we move on, let me ask you this: Do you know that Sefko Omerbasic was the number one man of the Islamic Community of the Republic of Herzegovina? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, I assume that he was of the Islamic faith. I don't know. I can't say. Now, I'm not an expert in Muslim affairs, and it seems that you are not either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, we can clarify that in due course, but let's go on to the next document, which is 3D 01045.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I said 3D 010145.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, it is the fifth document from the bottom, from the end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I've found the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Take a look at the document. It says that it is a report on the activities of the International Conference on the Protection of Human Rights in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the conference -- I'm going to go through this very quickly and you just tell me if what I'm saying is correct and you'll give your comments. At the end it says that the conference, at the invitation of the principal imam of the Zagreb mosque, Dr. Mustafa Ceric, held in Zagreb between the 18th and 19th of October, 1992, in order to inform the world of the war sufferings, especially of the Muslim population, it says. Follow the document, please. And then it says that the conference decided to establish an Executive Board, and once again the task was to coordinate the political and humanitarian aid to the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as to work on spreading the truth about the crimes committed against the Muslim people. And then at the bottom we see the names of the people who attended. I don't need to read all the names. Well, it says Muhamed Ghazali, Egypt. So we have Egypt, Qatar, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, et cetera, et cetera. Mustafa Pricanic, Bosnia-Herzegovina; Mustafa Ceric, Bosnia-Herzegovina; and al-Fatih Husanain from the Sudan. Now, on the following page, madam, it says that the meeting made the following decisions, et cetera, et cetera, and it says that Seikh Muhamed Ghazali should speak about the importance of the Muslim world. They were getting ready for a tour to establish a fund for the assistance -- for assistance to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the sum a billion US dollars. $1 billion US is the figure quoted. And then in continuation, it once again says that the Bosnian Muslims should be helped in all respects, and then we have a series of receptions that took place. That's on page 3. King al-Fatih Husanain, and then it says the importance of Bosnian Muslims for the Islamic world and the responsibility of all the Muslims in the world to help them, to render assistance. And then towards the end of that paragraph, in order to stop the persecution and killing of the Bosnian Muslims. And then it says that Salim Sabic asked that Saudi Arabia take part with a donation, initial donation, of $400 million US. Now, if you look at the very end, you will see the signature of the secretary in Jeddah, in 1992, Dr. Al-Fatih Husanain, on the 19th of October, and Dr. Mustafa Ceric. Do you know about Dr. Mustafa Ceric? Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Dr. Mustafa Ceric. I can't, of course, confirm that they are the original signatures, but I can see that there are signatures on that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now take a look at the next document, which is 3D 01046.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And in that document -- first of all, for the record, I'd just like to state that I have two binders full of documents from the Austrian and German police that conducted an investigation into the bank accounts in Vienna and Munich where this money was paid into, and Ms. Senka Nozica yesterday showed us something along those lines, in something that appeared in the paper Slobodna Bosna published in Sarajevo about just how much money was deposited into these private accounts and who controlled the accounts. We'll go through the document, but let me just ask you, madam, do you know about the existence of these organisations in Austria and Germany, where this money was siphoned into, the money given by the Islamic countries to the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be more specific in your question, in formulating your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, we have had a long speech on the previous document, and the only question asked was whether the witness knows about Dr. Mustafa Ceric. I think we should also know -- Witness, did you know about this conference that was held in Jeddah?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this or any other report on this conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this period, no. After the war, well, the media, the press, they published some things and I saw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, the media that you saw in Sarajevo, the papers you read, the newspapers, didn't they refer to several billion dollars that were received by way of assistance to the Muslim people from these states, from this conference that I read this document about?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is what the newspapers wrote after the war. That's the period that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, after the war.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's when I found out. That's why I'm asking you to be specific.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you learned from the media published in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the war that there were more and more revelations - now, whether all this is true or not, that's a different question - that several billion was received in these accounts.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I read.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Okay. So let's look at document 3D 01046.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says here that at the President Hotel in Geneva, a meeting was held that was attended by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, Ejub Ganic, Haris Silajdzic and al-Fatih Husanain, the director of the TWRA organisation. Have you ever heard of this organisation and also the aid that it provided to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And they made a decision that two other members should be included, Irfan Ljevakovic and Djordjevic Dervis, and that they were establishing a bank. Did you know that a bank was being established?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a document that I received in two binders, and that's what the German police was dealing with and got this from Mr. Pavlovic. Another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, yesterday, we saw how this money perhaps got into Zagreb. In terms of this organisation, the people that belonged to this organisation, did you ever get money in your own hands to distribute this money to refugees and other people?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not and people from the BH embassy did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of this money was ever received by the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please look at the next document, 3D 01048.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is: As for the ports that assistance to Bosnia-Herzegovina came to, was one of them Ploce?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to be. I guess it was. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Does my question mean anything to you if I ask you whether more than 600 million tonnes of freight were transported from that harbour to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look at this. This arrived from Saudi Arabia. We'll skip the figures, but I'm telling you the following: They say, rather, "Donations to Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where it is that you're reading in from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the left, under the Arab line, the second paragraph. It says --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. I don't have to confirm that I see what you are reading out. I really cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, this little bit up here in the upper left-hand corner. Nobody's asking you to read the Arabic writing because nobody here can read Arabic.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is it you're reading this from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I see what's written there. Yes. Shipment --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says that it is donations to Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what's written here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't see Ploce.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Ploce, Croatia, underneath. Can't you see it, Ploce, Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say so in the same paragraph. Well, probably it does, but it's not important whether I see it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that the assistance that was received, say, from Saudi Arabia -- we don't have time to go into this now, but I would show you a film where, which is only natural, the holy Koran is being distributed, many copies, and that this aid was given only to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then we are going to skip this. If you don't know about this then there is no reason for us to deal with this. Concerning the harbour of Ploce, there's lots of documents. What about Rijeka, Split, other harbours in Croatia? Did they receive aid from Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You don't know. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, how much time have we got left? Five minutes now. Four.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now let us just clarify some small details that are nevertheless important for me, so let's deal with that in these four minutes. However, it's important to me. Do you know this big group of refugees that came from Gorazde to the mosque in Zagreb at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that an enormous number of refugees came to the mosque, in front of the mosque. As for the people from Gorazde, I can't remember them specifically, but I remember lots and lots of people in front of mosque.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Was the mosque a central focal point from where refugees were distributed in various centres?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. For me primarily it was the focal point, the centre where refugees were left, refugees who were driven to the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But then they were taken to places where they resided.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know of one detail, for instance? Do you know the name of Dr. Juraj Njavro?
