utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, that when a big group of people from Gorazde came, President Tudjman asked Juraj Njavro, a refugee from Vukovar, to go and talk to these people, to help them in the situation that they were in? Do you know of this detail?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't know about that, but I am not surprised. I believe that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Praljak please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that in Zagreb only there were only 16 centres for Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but there were many refugee centres; that I do know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did many Croatian citizens give their houses, especially their weekend cottages where they did not live, to refugees for their use?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thousands and thousands of such cases?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience is that it is very many. I don't know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How about a fundamental question now that we're dealing with refugees? For instance, when 500.000 refugees come from Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia, do you agree that at one point there were 500.000 refugees?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Does these -- along with these refugees, don't thieves come in, criminals, whores, whatever a person can find in a group of 500.000 people?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind, it is only logical to assume that this kind of a sample includes representatives of all kinds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, logical. Can you assume that they caused a great deal of crime?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can assume all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You were involved in marketing propaganda?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not propaganda. Marketing, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know who Dr. Tanja Kesic is? This is an intimate question.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name sounds familiar, but I obviously don't know her very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: She was at your university when you got your diploma.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not at the department that I was at.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: There are studies of psychology there, that department, I'm sure of that. Among these refugees, among this refugee population who did not have much information about what was going on back home, how many stories were bandied about, terrible stories? Imagine --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly what was going on, but it is only logical to assume that there was a lot of imagination involved, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. We can break off at this point. Thank you, madam, and we will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've counted. Mr. Praljak, you've already spent one hour, so theoretically you have no time left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have half an hour from the attorney of Mr. Berko Pusic and 20 minutes from Ms. Senka Nozica. Oh, sorry, Vesna Alaburic. Well, anyway, please. So I have about 50 minutes or so left to go through some important matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have a 20-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to proceed with the cross-examination, but before giving the floor to Mr. Praljak, let me make one comment on behalf of the Chamber. We'd like to ask the witness and Mr. Praljak to speak much slower. I told you a few weeks ago that the translation services told us that we produce in this trial more than 20 per cent of transcript pages than the other trials because everybody is speaking extremely fast - 20 per cent more pages of transcript than the other trials. But in this case, with Mr. Praljak asking questions and the witness answering these questions, the number of words spoken is so huge that the interpreters and the court reporter can't follow. I was told that you can take a maximum of 240 per minute, and you are currently speaking at a rate of 300 words a minute. So please try to slow down. Think of those assisting us. I, myself, I'm able to follow you, of course, but think of the translators. Think of the court reporter. Please try to slow down. My fellow Judge wants to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Mr. Praljak resumes, I'd like to have one point of clarification. I'm looking at the documents you've given us, Mr. Praljak, and I look at document 3D 01046. 3D 01046. This is related to a meeting that took place on the 14th of September, 1993, at the President Hotel in Geneva. Where does this document come from? I'm asking the question because I can see here at the bottom the name of Pavlovic. And apparently the document was generated in Munich in 1995, on the 7th of December, 1995, but I do not see any reference number, any stamps. So I'd like to know where this document comes from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this terrible struggle to get documents in order to shed as much light as possible on this entire case, I managed to obtain two binders of the investigation conducted by the Austrian and German federal police about money-laundering through the organisation mentioned in the document. Pavlovic is the translator of these documents. I have these two binders of documents from the Austrian and German police, but I think that this information comes from the Prosecution as well, because this did come up in a particular case. Of course, I'm going to make this available to the Court through a witness who is going to be better versed in the matter, regardless of whether this witness will be called by the Prosecution or the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, we're going to continue. Thank you for your answers so far. Just two more brief questions. In your department you did not have any employed psychologists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, throughout the time while you dealt with this subject matter, do you know that there was a single murder, rape, serious crime among the refugee population? Let us not go into petty crime. But do you know about serious crimes committed within the refugee population from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us now look at another document that I still owe you. P 01062. This is a Prosecution document. The page is 0328-7247 -- 7207.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the Prosecutor's bundle of documents, could someone just open that document? 10062. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says, "Professor Dr. Adalbert Rebic. Dear Mrs. Turkovic," et cetera. I'm just interested in the second paragraph. He says to her, "If a home is destroyed and if the person affected brings a certificate from the club" -- or, rather, the social --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Help me. Help me. Could you please find the paragraph that you're reading? I cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: There's two documents. The second paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. It says here, "Unless the person concerned brings a certificate from the club" --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that that's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm asking yet again. Do you know that Professor Adalbert Rebic's office recognised certificates issued by the local clubs that were established on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that in a way represented the municipal authorities of those towns that the refugees came from, Zavidovici, Bihac, Maglaj, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he wrote that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that he recognised these documents?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of cases when they did not recognise those documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you tell the Honourable Trial Chamber how many such cases occurred, when, and so on?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no statistics. I did not consider that to be indispensable. I don't have systematically recorded information. I cannot give you statistics. I don't have any.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, you know what you know. Please let us move on to document 3D 01030. 3D 01030. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Because time is so brief, I'm going to ask you some questions very quickly. Please look at page 143. 143.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can someone please help me with this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, look at the map --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 143 is the page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 143 is the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I am afraid we will have a problem here, because those maps, pictures, which were copied in colour were not assigned e-court numbers. So they're all in this folder [Interpretation] 3D 01030, but not every page is marked. So perhaps Mr. Praljak should explain what page he's referring to in terms of the heading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I be of assistance? I have the page in front of me on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the monitor. Thank you. That will do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Praljak please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Spring 1992, April, May. As the aggression already started, that is to say, of the JNA and the army of Republika Srpska, there were columns of refugees at that time, most of them Muslims, and they were moving towards Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the HZ HB, which had been established at that time as well, as the HVO was building a road called the Salvation Road through Mount Vran because all the other roads down south had been severed by the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of the Salvation Road.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that these refugees, first and foremost, were put up in the territory of Herzegovina - Posusje, Livno, Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm going to phrase my question this way: At first, most of the people who were fleeing, did they think that the war would go on for 15 days, a month, a month and a half? Was that the prevalent feeling among the people at the time? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that for that reason people were not rushing into Croatia at that time but they, rather, stayed on in these places that were not all that safe and they hoped that they would be going back home soon? Part of the people, that is.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds logical to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask -- all right. Well, these maps. Well, I don't know how many there are, but I'm going to ask you the following: Do you know that refugees from Eastern Herzegovina - Nevesinje, Trebinje and so on - Muslims, were taken care in the municipalities of Mostar, Capljina? Roughly at that time, in 1992, it was about 20.000 people.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can testify that at the directorate we tried to obtain this information, but while I was in Bosnia we did not have this information or the relevant data. There were stories.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that towards the end of May or in mid-May, rather, the army of Republika Srpska had reached the eastern bank of the Neretva River and had expelled the entire non-Serb population from the eastern bank of the Neretva River?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And that that population was taken care of on the territory HZ HB - Grude, Western Mostar - part of them went to Croatia, to the seaside, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right, Mrs. Krajsek, if you don't know, you don't know. We're taking these things in the order they came up. If you don't know, that's fine. Now, another question: Would you agree with me when I say that all the available hotel accommodation along the Adriatic coast and all the other holiday centres, trade union ones, whatever, were placed at the disposal of the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina and of course Croatia as well?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me again that this was more than 100 facilities, hotels, holiday homes, whatever, camps, things like that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't ask me to confirm numbers. There was a large number, but I can't be specific as to the exact number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday, some figures were presented here related to the Croatian government, et cetera, but let's look at one thing. Do you know that those hotel companies were paid by the Croatian government to accommodate, send some food, et cetera, to accommodate these people, and they paid 2 euros per day, the equivalent of 2 euros per day, per person per day?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm sure you read about it later on. But do you know that all these hotels and holiday facilities with this kind of economic policy were completely devastated? Nothing was invested in them for years and their value dropped to 25 to 30 per cent of what their value was before the war. They were in such poor repair.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during the war, did you ever hear of me, my name, surname? Did you know about me? Did you know of me?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure when I first heard of you, whether that was during the war or after the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Probably after the Old Bridge, because that's when everybody heard of me. Now, in coming into contact with the refugees, did you perhaps learn that in my weekend cottage I had taken in 13 Muslim refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from them, but I did hear that from others.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. And since I communicated with them because they needed to be fed and kept warm, do you know that those refugees received certain resources from the representatives of the Iranian, let's say, authorities in their hands personally every month?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You don't know about that. Right. And you don't know that this -- that it was the Iranians that just handed this money out to Muslims alone, never to Croats. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we go back a bit? You asked me about the refugees that were put up in your house, is that what you mean, in your holiday home?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, I mean generally.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, I do know, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to go into private session for a moment because I have to name names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Your Honour. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, were there many people from the former Yugoslavia working in Western European countries as guest workers?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: About 350.000 Croats from Croatia? Would that be the kind of figure?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I persistently keep telling you that I'm not somebody who is well-versed in figures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You don't know how many Bosniaks worked in the countries of Western Europe?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But did you know that many refugees were staying with friends, like they were with me, in order to contact their own people who worked in France, Belgium, et cetera, and then would travel with their Yugoslav passport to go to those people they knew in third countries without having previously registered as refugees?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know when the conflicts broke out - we're not going to discuss who expelled whom and so on - but anyway, that after the fall of Jajce, when the Serbs took control of Jajce, a large number of Croats and some Muslims moved towards Croatia? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the numbers of refugees who fled from Visoko, Sarajevo, Kresevo, Mostar, Capljina, those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I might have known that, that data was inaccessible, so I didn't have that information to hand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You say that you talked to refugees who had fled from Zenica and Kakanj in Pinete, and my question to you is this: Do you know that in the Kakanj municipality, on the 18th of May, in Kakanj, in 1993, nine Croats were killed? I'm going to enumerate all these cases, and then you can tell me what you knew. On the 12th of June, in Trubaci [phoen], three Croats were killed. In Tesevo Ljesem Balici [phoen], on the 13th of June, 1993, seven Croats were killed. In Slapasnice, on the 13th of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I do not quite see much purpose in this because the witness has numerous times told us that she does not remember figures, and it might be more useful if you could sort of put one more global question which she could answer, probably.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: According to the information that was published and collected, in Kakanj municipality, 55 Croats were killed before they were expelled. I won't go into who did that - that's not my topic - but did the refugees talk to you about any of these incidents, tell you about that, in Pinete?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, when you spent time there in Doljani, you told us about that yesterday, and I have facts and figures for 1.147 Croats killed in 21 municipalities from Capljina towards the north, in all the different places in that area, Uzdol, Grabovica, Konjic, Dusina, et cetera. Now, while you were there, through the embassy did you have information about the crimes that certain people from the BH army, for instance, committed against the Croats?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the public information media, that's where I learnt about that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, in a brochure that I have prepared for these proceedings, you will find 290 religious facilities that were damaged, destroyed. This includes churches and so on. And some members of the BH army committed these crimes in the territory that they took control of. So did you have any information about that during the time that you spent there?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the papers and information media informed about it, then I would have heard about them, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that when the war flared up between the BH army and the HVO, the situation amongst the refugees, both Croats and Bosniaks, deteriorated in certain areas?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mrs. Krajsek, did you know that the authorities of the Republic of Croatia were then faced with the fact that these two belligerent parties had to be separated to avoid an internationality conflict because there were casualties on both sides? So do you know that the authorities had to step in?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now some more documents, and in that same document number on page -- 3D 01030, and the page is 197, 3D 26-0197. They are two letters written by Mrs. Bisera Turkovic and sent, we'll see to whom when you find them.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't find those numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, could you help us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will come up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I'll just read out the basics.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The first letter was written on the 19th of April, 1994, and you'll see on the second page that somebody signed for Mrs. Bisera Turkovic, and the letter was sent to the UN Human Rights Centre, to international organisations, the ICRC, and so on and so forth. And the title says, "UNHCR," to the attention of Mr. Jacques Moucher, High Commissioner. Have you found that? Do you see the letter?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it on the screen but I couldn't find it in my documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's fine. So she's relating to Bosniaks going on to third countries to resettle, relocate into third countries.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, madam, did you know that the UNHCR, as it says here, the staff of the UNHCR was collecting together refugees and explaining to them that conditions were not yet right for safe return to Mostar because they say that Mostar was not a safe place for either the Croats or the Serbs and that they couldn't go to Mostar, that they should be patient, and not to be taken in by the convoys that were prepared for a return journey. And on the 19th of April -- well, my question is this: Do you know that the Washington Accords had been signed and that the two sides, two forces, the BH army and the HVO, had been separated and the war had actually ceased? Do you know about that? After the agreement had been signed?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So after the Split agreement and the separation of forces, an organised return was supposed to begin, and the UNHCR says here or, rather, Mrs. Turkovic says: "If the Croats revoke your status of refugees, then we will organise your departure to third countries." And she goes on to say --

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I do apologise, but I just can't follow you, looking at the document. Either read exactly what it says or it's your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. So you read the third paragraph from the top, then.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We also have information about the continuous activities of the UNHCR in collective refugee centres: Gasinci, Savudrija, Ucka, Varazdin Obonjan, and others relating to the everyday work of the UNHCR on the relocation and displacement of Bosnian refugees (with the regulated refugee status) from the republic of Croatia to third countries." I know that. I know the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You know the document?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: As far as I understand things, you are complaining about the UNHCR, why they are working on relocating Muslims to third countries.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not complaining. I'm just asking them why.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to the next document. The next document, 3D 26-0199 is the page number.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we dealing with your binder now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but just repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please try and give us the page number in English so the registrar can put them on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it goes. 3D 26-0199.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the English is 0258.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I suggest something? Could someone confirm for me that we have the right document on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the monitor right now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, this document that you've been looking at so far, 199 is just a few pages behind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it. Thank you to everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Ms. Krajsek, you see it's the same thing. Zagreb, on the 19th of April. I don't know who it was who signed this. Is it you or somebody else? Signing for Bisera Turkovic. Bisera Turkovic is writing to Dr. Adalbert Rebic.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the document. I wrote it. The secretary signed it on behalf of Mrs. Turkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Then we don't need much comment. In the first paragraph, we see that she says: "Information on increasing number of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian citizens who, through the help the UNHCR, keep arriving on the border of the Republic of Croatia with the aim of reaching third countries." And she says: "We particularly appreciate and accept the offered cooperation between the Office for Expelled Persons and Refugees and the Embassy by which control of work of organisations would be introduced, those dealing with forwarding civilians from Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Doesn't this show that the UNHCR, and there are many, many other documents, the UNHCR was dealing in a continuous and organised manner on getting intellectuals and other younger people from Bosnia-Herzegovina to third countries?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is obvious on the basis of this is that I highly appreciate and accept the cooperation offered, bearing in mind the information provided that the UNHCR is doing what you've said just now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Krajsek, do you know that many others as well - we cannot go through all the documents - were doing the same thing as the UNHCR was doing?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now tell me the following: Do you know of a single case where the Croatian state by force, against the will of refugees, returned a single refugee to another country across the Croatian border, north, south, east, west?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat that question. You're asking me about a refugee or --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We're talking about refugees in the Republic of Croatia. Do you have any example where an institution of the Republic of Croatia took two, three, five, ten refugees, and against their own will relocated them to Bosnia-Herzegovina, Hungary, Austria, Slovenia, anywhere?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have such information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: What information?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a given period of time - I don't want to refer to dates without the relevant documents - a great deal of information was coming to the embassy to the effect that the Croatian police were stopping refugees, especially in Zagreb, taking away their refugee papers, arresting them, putting them up at Remetinec, I think. But there are documents about that. I reported on that. For me, these are examples of why I'm giving you an affirmative answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, now there is an area that we will have to deal with very quickly, regrettably, and I cannot really clarify that with you. At one moment you mentioned 450 and at another moment 120, Muslims who went missing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish I could see the document itself. I remember that particular figure, for instance, but I don't know what the other terms I stated were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 65 and 67 are the paragraphs of your statement, and you say that there are 120 arrested Muslims. And you also mentioned that in the Rama action they were being arrested. So I'm going to put my question again. Do you know that the action Rama was carried out by the Croatian police at the request of the police of the HZ HB to arrest those Croats from Rama and the surrounding area who had committed some crimes or who were suspects of having committed certain crimes? Do you know that the Rama action pertained to Croats who had fled to the Republic of Croatia and were suspected of having committed certain crimes, convoys, all sorts of things?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know upon whom this action had a reflection. I don't know why it was taken in the first place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, this is how I'm going to phrase my question: Do you know that there were training centres of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia? At Borongaj, Sljeme, Jastrebarsko, Pljesivica, Kutina, Sisak, and so on and so forth? Do you know these facts, that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia had its own training grounds, training centres?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday you mentioned some name. Do you know Asim Kamber?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall such a name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You remember Hajrudin Osmanagic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hajrudin Osmanagic was an attache. He had something to do with the military.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. He was the military attache of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Zoran Poprzenovic , was he the same after him?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Hasan Efendic?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No. Actually, I'm not giving you the position, but I know the name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that over 30 persons had diplomatic passports and that they were doing all the military work for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right, madam. Okay, okay. Please look at document -- well, I'm just going to ask you this very briefly: Do you know how many units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were established in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or, rather, Croatia and were sent to the front line in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know whether out of these 120 individuals that you mention and the 450 who you somehow lost sight of, do you have any names from the ranks of these people so that I can look it up in the documentation and see whether they were escorted by the Croatian police and went to one of these units that were established, whether they went to the Bihac front, to the front in Central Bosnia? Do you have any names of any of these people who went missing, as far as you are concerned?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I did not refer to the names in my reports, and if I did not attach any lists, that means that I never had these names.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, well, regrettably, you don't know this, but this is roughly how I'm going to put it: Assistance in arming the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Republic of Croatia. Did you know that there was assistance in arming the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was carried out by the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So it is all in vain that I went through 3.000 -- 3.238 documents, if I am to quantify all this information, quantified information contained in tables. In a way, it would be in vain if I were to go through all of this with you.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were to ask me anything that was not within my own line of work, you would be asking me that in vain, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that vis-a-vis Bihac there was always an airlift from the Republic of Croatia towards the Coralici airport near Bihac? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, I don't want to feel embarrassed in any way. When you ask me whether I know about something, I give an answer on the basis of my own knowledge or I point out that I heard through the media. If you want to go with me through documents that I had never seen, I really cannot help you with that and I cannot give you an affirmative answer. I don't want you to understand me to be an uncooperative person.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No. No, madam. I know that they were -- well, I mean I want to ask you: Jastrebarsko, Borongaj, Popovac, Duboki Jarak, Ploce, did you ever hear of these being bases where the Croatian army had the right to store weapons which were afterwards sent to the front in Sarajevo, Srebrenica, Gorazde, for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Well, yes. Just a second, please. I have a sub-file here. Weapons packaged in food packaging and put into UNHCR vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I've tried not to get on my feet today, but I am wondering at this point whether, as a courtesy to Ms. Alaburic, it would be better to let her use her time than to waste time on irrelevant questions to this witness, who, for the last half hour, has basically said, "I don't know anything about that. I don't know about military matters," but Mr. Praljak continues to put questions to her. I don't think it's a wise use of time. When you say, You have an hour, that that means you can waste an hour and then Ms. Alaburic is not going to have time to put perhaps, I hope, good and relevant questions to the witness. So I just suggest that out of courtesy, out of courtesy Mr. Praljak might want to leave time, instead of asking irrelevant questions, for his colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it is indisputable that until now you gave the Defence the right to allocate their own time amongst themselves as best they could. Ms. Alaburic said that she needed 50 minutes, and Mr. Praljak knows that and he will abide by that. However, as for what the Prosecutor said just now, that Praljak has been asking time and again this witness about things she didn't know and that therefore this was a waste of time and the Prosecutor is therefore worried about that, I have to say that Praljak has relevant subjects to deal with, and the witness either knows or doesn't know. I personally expected the witness to respond to some questions saying that she didn't know anything about it, but she, on the contrary, gave some very detailed and specific information. So Praljak takes into account the fact that the witness was, A, in the embassy that had a great deal of information; B, she lived in Croatia where she could, in different ways, find out about different things, not to mention the period while she was still in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it is only reasonable for Praljak to ask questions. It is not a fishing expedition. Sometimes it is only reasonable that the witness will know the answer. Sometimes she will not know. But Praljak is entitled to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I just want to be clear again. What I heard Ms. Alaburic say earlier today is that she would like as much additional time as possible. That's what she asked the Chamber for earlier. I also indicate that I do expect a reasonable amount of redirect time. And I do object, I do object, when the rights of other parties, including Ms. Alaburic and myself, are prejudiced by the waste of time on irrelevant questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, obviously on military matters this witness cannot give any answers. You now have 10 minutes left. You can continue asking questions by which she can only reply by, "I don't know," and these are questions that you have already put to others. It's up to you. You have 10 minutes, and 10 minutes only.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. You see, the lady said in her statement that once 120 people went missing and on another occasion 450 people went missing, and that they were taken by the Croatian police. That is a crime, if it remains written that way. Of course I cannot go through the entire documents; that won't work. But does she know how many people in Croatia were equipped, trained, in BH army units and how they went to Bihac and Central Bosnia and how many of them got killed as they were going to Bihac? This is based on lists, et cetera, so this is something that the lady knew.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I know that you knew of that, but you were not aware of what their fate was after that. So that is what I wanted to check. That is number one. Number two, if I'm talking about weapons that were packed into food packaging on UNHCR trucks, which was regular practice, and in organised fashion tins were opened and, with the presence of the Croatian army, myself included -- well, this has something to do with the convoy from Split, because the lady said that the convoy stood there for as long as it did, so I know and I'm asking the lady whether she knows - and again I'm going to show you the document - that in these tins there were weapons. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right, madam. Thank you very much. Now please look at 3D 01031.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, Your Honours, the answer that the lady does not know is also a relevant answer, to see what her overall knowledge was in it order to draw certain conclusions on the conduct of all segments of the Croatian state, myself included, and also these people who sit here and who stand accused of a joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, please, look at any document. Just look at it. Look at the first one. It says, "On the day," whatever, the 24th of June, 1993, and UNHCR, 01236 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the document. It is very hard to find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is that what is written there? 3D 01031. And the page is 262, actually.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the page in front of me, which is on the monitor now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Do you see the truck?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are saying is written here, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm going to skip all the other documents. As far as Bihac is concerned, there is 1.200 of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, this document that you have just shown, which is 262 in B/C/S, I see that there is some kind of note at the end of the document saying that there is good cooperation on the line of the HVO. What exactly does this mean? It looks like weapons are going to cross into Bosnia-Herzegovina in UNHCR trucks that have false registration plates, but everything is done in full cooperation with the HVO. Is that what the last sentence means? And, Witness, please, you were at the embassy. Were you aware of the fact that weapons could cross into Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Republic of Croatia in full cooperation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no information linked to any military operations and cooperation. Information like that never reached me, nor would it have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you know nothing. Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from the documents I could show that over 40 UNHCR trucks did take weapons to Bihac in Central Bosnia and later on even more and there was this cooperation. There are many, many documents about that. But never mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, look at the map that we're showing you now, the big map next to you on the easel. On that map I have written in -- indicated what we're interested in. Towards the end of 1992, the amount of free territory left in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You see the areas occupied in the Republic of Croatia. It was a map that appeared in the papers. Would that roughly be it?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not qualified at all to answer that question, whether it is or is not. And to be quite frank, regardless of my glasses, I really can't see it clearly. I never knew anything about that, Mr. Praljak. Those are things that I just do not know about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. But let me just ask you this, I'll put it this way: Can you confirm that it was very difficult and almost impossible to accommodate refugees in the town of Osijek and its surrounding parts because it was near to the area that was bombed?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know which period you have in mind, but generally speaking, I think that that statement is logical.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm going to give you some other names of towns. Vinkovac, because of the vicinity of the battlefield; is that right? Slavonski Brod, another place. Sisak, Karlovac, Ogulin, Dubrovnik, because it was destroyed, and so on.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: There were some refugees in Sisak but I don't really know what you're asking me. Would you restate your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Because of the very serious shelling of the town of Osijek and all the civilians that were killed and so on, so in town and the surrounding parts, because we mentioned Sisak, et cetera, and the refugees there, but anyway, in those towns, the one that I mentioned, they were places where refugees couldn't be put up because there was combat activity going on, because the Serbs were shooting Sisak, Karlovac, Ogulin, Slavonski Brod, Vinkovci. Is that something that you would agree with? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, with the exception of Sisak and all those other places you mentioned, I don't know that any refugees were put up there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. So there was just Istria, Dalmatia, Sibenik -- well, Sibenik wasn't very secure. There were very few places left. Zadar, too.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: There was just one ferry link between the north and south of Croatia, the destroyed bridge on Pag island, and you had to use the ferry; right? So all the refugees had to take this ferry-line?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, my last question, madam. Regardless of all the problems -- sometimes there were 800.000 refugees at one point in time, with a third of the territory occupied and territories where refugees could not be housed. Now, everything you learnt before the war, after the war, during the war, everything that Croatia did, Croatia made an exceptionally strong effort to take care of the refugees coming in from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croats, Muslims, not differentiating between the two at all except for perhaps some rare examples. But they acted as a civilised state where the rule of law prevailed, that that is how they acted, that they acted in conformity with that.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an attache for refugees, unfortunately, I was the person in place where the information about the problems reached me. As the attache for refugees, I can say regardless of the intentions or wishes - I don't want to enter into the realm; they might have been good intentions - but the information that reached me was information about the problems that the refugees faced and where they required additional protection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Tell me now, madam, did you check this information out? If you were told that somebody attacked them and so on, did you have the possibility of checking out the information they gave you? And did you, for the lady you mentioned on the island of Obonjan, for example, the mother with the two children, did you send in a request to the Croatian authorities to respond and to tell you what had happened and who had been expelled from Split? Did you ask for that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did they give you an answer?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, can we have the letter where you sent out your request?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you already have that document, that it's included in the documents, that letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, do you know that on the island of Obonjan, even before the refugees arrived, that there is no ferry even to the present day, that there was just a ferry-line only at the time when the refugees there? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you for your cooperation. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. May I just, Your Honour, ask that the map receive an IC number, because the lady did say she knew about the towns, and the legend is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a number for the IC map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the map will become Exhibit IC 607.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, one question. In this embassy where you were working in Zagreb, we know that you were in charge of refugees, but I assume that other people were dealing with other sectors, notably, military matters. So as far as you're aware, was there a military attache in the embassy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. In the documents prepared by Mr. Praljak, I see that there's one called Hajrudin Osmanagic. Does this ring a bell? Hajrudin Osmanagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did meet Mr. Osmanagic when he took over the post of attache, military attache.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So we have a document, number 3D 260290, coming from the military attache and sent to the commander of the 3rd Corps, Ramiz Turkovic. This is a very straightforward document. It says that weapons and equipment are coming on trucks with UNHCR registration plates. So you were in charge of refugees, and I'm sure if this had been known it might have created a problem. So did the military attache -- did you know about this? Did somebody talk to you about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He never said anything to you about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, but we have the document here which states that weapons were being sent in August 1993 to Bosnia-Herzegovina on trucks with UNHCR registration plates, and we actually have the registration plates, the numbers. This is document 3D 26-0290, under 3D 0131. I'm sure the Judges will scrutinise this document. Now, Mrs. -- oh, my colleague Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, in the same line as the President's question, I would like to know whether -- in your embassy in Croatia you told us that there were about 30 people working, among which a military attache. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These 30 people, of course, had diplomatic passports, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. All I know is that not everybody who worked for the embassy, whether in the embassy or in the consular offices, enjoyed diplomatic status. I don't know how many of them did have diplomatic passports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right. But did your embassy have a directory with the names of all people that had a diplomatic passport from your own country, people who had this passport but who were working in Croatia, who were residing permanently in Croatia? Of course, you also had a consular department in charge of the citizens living in Croatia. Was there a directory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, just a question on the document I was mentioning earlier, 20290. Where does it come from? Was it disclosed by the Prosecution or did you obtain it directly during your investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we go into private session, Your Honours, for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor before we take a break. But I see that Ms. Nozica is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before my colleague takes the floor, I would like to provide Judge Mindua with an explanation when he asked about the origins of the document that Mr. Praljak presented and which dates back to 1995 and was signed by Mr. Pavlovic. Yesterday, in court I showed a document, 2D 00498 was the number, and as far as I know Judge Mindua was provided with my binder today, but it is a set of documents or, rather, a complete document that we were provided under Rule 68 by the Prosecutor. Now, if you leaf through that entire document, and referring to page 0328-4950, you will find identical documents to those shown by Mr. Praljak from 1995 and signed by Mr. Pavlovic. And from this binder you can see that that is part of the documentation which was quite obviously used in Austria for the investigation against certain persons and organisations. So let me repeat: This document was disclosed by the Prosecutor, provided to us by the Prosecutor, by way of assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to go back to what Mr. Praljak has told us. At one point he said, We had to send material, including weapons, to Bihac. No one recognised that they were completely closed in. Does that mean that the Croat republic was also, I suppose, using UNHCR or UNHCR-disguised vehicles for such transports of military material?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, hold on. Before there's an answer to that question, Your Honour, are you seeking to -- are you placing General Praljak under the obligation of answering questions, in other words, testifying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm giving him the opportunity to clarify a statement that he has made and that is on the record and which might be interpreted in different manners. I would like to avoid a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. At this point, as long as the understanding is that, first of all, questions are not evidence, questions that are posed or even statements that attorneys make, whether it's on cross or direct, opening or closing, are not evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's understood. And given that Mr. Praljak is representing himself, of course, and I understand that the Prosecutor here is mumbling, as usual, but given that there are attitude is that Mr. Praljak is testifying, I think we need to be absolutely clear that, first and foremost, one, he's not under oath; two, he has no obligation to testify. If he does choose to testify, then the Prosecutor can ask all the questions, as can the Chamber. So I think that we need to have some clarification that -- that you're asking him to clarify a statement, but I think we're on dangerous ground at this point of somehow transgressing into some sort of violation of rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, we are going to waste a lot of precious time. This is totally irrelevant. Mr. Scott, let's waste some more time. Please have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't do it. I'm not going to waste time. But I would like to come back to the topic. But I don't think it's correct to let other people have the floor and then make a comment like that to the Prosecution about wasting time. I'm sorry, Your Honour, with great respect, I object to that. But based on your instruction, I will not go further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to tell you why we are wasting time. Judge Trechsel asked Mr. Praljak to clarify one of the answers he'd given. It was a point of clarification. It was not a question; it was a point of clarification. And Mr. Praljak, if he chooses to do so, can answer, give a clarification. We are not entering a discussion here. We are just trying to understand what Mr. Praljak was saying, and he was perfectly entitled to answer or not, to clarify or not. Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very gladly. UNHCR trucks, fuel trucks with double bottoms, were used for transporting weapons to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina towards Bihac non-stop, along with two aircraft provided by the Croatian government. For those parts of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were outside the territory of the HVO, when there was a conflict, then it was more difficult for convoys to get through because it had to be explained to the boys that this could not be done. And then it was loaded onto the trucks with full knowledge of the Croatian state because it was done on our territory. These were original trucks. The people who were engaged in the transport, who were driving, knew about that. I mean, I can testify about that for days, about all of this when my turn comes. Mr. Kovacic is defending me properly, but I have to say that I'm doing this, for all the efforts I have made over the past 10 years, to obtain the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I would like to make two points. The first one, that this question was asked by the President, also by Judge Mindua, and myself, I would like to add my voice to know more about the origin of the documents. And, actually, Mr. Praljak has spoken about it, but I am still, in a way, doubtful as far as the authenticity of the documents is concerned. So I believe that this issue should be further studied. That was number one. Number two, I really feel that since we have to finish after the break, a quarter to 2.00, I would like to know now what is the actual situation with the time allocation, because we should, first of all -- probably we should ask the Prosecution what time they would like to have, and after this, we have to decide how to proceed, because we have lost a lot of time now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as time is concern, I believe Ms. Alaburic needs 15 to 20 minutes. Then we'll have the break. How much time will you need, Mr. Scott, for re-examination? Because after the break we'll have only 45 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on past experience, I'm going to say 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So it's still feasible. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Krajsek, good afternoon to you. First of all, I would like us to clarify one answer you gave to General Praljak's question that was recorded in today's transcript, page 63. I'm not going to have any documents. We are simply going to talk. General Praljak put a question to you about a single example to the effect that the Croatian authorities deported a Bosniak to a third country, a Bosniak refugee to third country, Hungary, Austria, Slovenia, whatever. In response to that question, you said that sometimes the Croatian police would arrest a Bosniak and arrest them in Remetinec. Do you remember that answer that you gave? My question is: Remetinec, to the best of my knowledge, is in Zagreb. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I conclude that your answer is not the answer that General Praljak put to you, because the question had to do with forced deportation of a Bosniak, a Bosniak refugee from Croatia into a third country.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive any such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, madam, Ms. Krajsek, let's just clarify what Remetinec is. Tell us, Remetinec is the regular investigative prison in Zagreb where people are detained as they are arrested. So it is a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that is the situation, but I can give an explanation in terms of mass deportations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since you heard that I have very little time, if we do have some time left, I will be very glad to let you explain. Ms. Krajsek, I would like us to explain the question of birth certificates.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the interpreters please interpret "Krsni List" not a birth certificate but literally as baptism, christening certificate, as proof of christening.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Ms. Krajsek, when you refer in your statement and here to christening certificates, you are referring to proof of christening?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Ms. Krajsek, did you ever see any regulation of the Republic of Croatia in which proof of christening was required for the exercise of any civil rights?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not look at these documents very much. It was my lawyer, the legal officer at the embassy, who did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did the legal officer tell you that he read any regulation of the Republic of Croatia in which proof of christening was a requirement for the exercise of any right?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what regulation that was?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can in general terms. A number of regulations, I cannot give you --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. What was the topic? What regulation was that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This had to do with the registration of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, their enrollment in regular schools in the Republic of Croatia. The required documentation included bringing proof of christening.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this did not pertain to secondary schools and universities and pre-school institutions?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We only focused on elementary education, primary education. I don't know whether it applied to the rest, but I'm talking about elementary education.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understand you properly now, in the words of your legal officer, you did not find out about any regulation that, in principle, would require proof of christening in Croatia to be a requirement for the exercise of any right? A christening certificate was only a requirement for enrolling children in elementary school, just that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I really have lost the thread of what it was that you were saying. Could you please repeat this once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we were to summarise, the legal officer you worked with and who followed regulations said that christening certificates were only required for the enrollment of children in elementary schools.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not go into legal regulations. He did not analyse other legal regulations. I know with certainty that he could not analyse all the regulations of the Republic of Croatia. He could and did analyse those regulations which possibly prevented the exercise of some of the rights that refugees should be entitled to in the host country.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Ms. Krajsek, since you lived in Croatia for a while, can we not agree that in Croatia there are atheists, there are people who quite simply do not go to the church or are not of the Christian faith and who quite simply had not been baptised and do not have any proof of christening?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of these people being denied the exercise of any human rights in the Republic of Croatia? Human rights, civil rights, and so on, in the Republic of Croatia. Have you ever heard of that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally you're talking about citizens? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, do you know that christenings are carried out in Catholic churches, Orthodox churches, Protestant churches, and other Christian churches.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please include the Orthodox church in my question because it is important for me to go on. So Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and other Christian churches. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when your legal officer was explaining this proof of christening to you, did he tell you that a proof of christening was required from a Catholic church or would one from the Orthodox church do as well?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not talk to me about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. You said to us today, and it was recorded on today's page 9, that in the school year of 1992-1993 there were no problems for enrolling Bosniak children who were refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in regular schools of the Republic of Croatia. Can we confirm that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive such information. We can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in view of this statement, could we conclude that your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal should be corrected to the effect that children of Bosniaks could not be enrolled in the regular Croatian schooling system for the mentioned school year of 1992-1993?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that I said something like that. In September 1992, one enrolled in school, so I could not have talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Ms. Krajsek, precisely because you, in your statement, did not specify what was going on in terms of school years, but you just have this general assessment which would lead us to believe that it pertains to all school years, I simply want to analyse it. So what you say in paragraph 25; namely, that the Bosnian Croat children were incorporated in the regular Croat schooling system, while for the Bosniaks you had to develop this net, I want to ask you now: In relation to your previous answer for the school year of 1992-1993, such an assessment would not be right. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we cannot. I believe that it is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Something seems to be wrong there. Tell me -- let me repeat: In the school year of 1992-1993, could Bosniak children enroll in the regular Croatian schooling system without any problems?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So in that school year they did not have to go to a special school network. They could be enrolled in regular Croatian schools.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had sufficient capacities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear counsel. She was speaking at the same time as the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That is why I want to conclude, in relation to paragraph 25, that children of refugees who were Bosniaks could not go to regular Croatian schools in 1992-1993. That statement, quite simply, is not correct and not accurate, because they could attend schools belonging to the regular school system, as you said to us just now.

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I claim that in 1992-1993, in that particular school year, a large number of children of Bosniak refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina were not included in the regular elementary education of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Ms. Krajsek, I suggest that we talk in the following way: First of all, let us see what it was that Bosniak children were entitled to, and then let us look at this together and see whether this right could be exercised due to the existing capacities, teachers, and so on and so forth. So right now we are talking about the rights of Bosniak children. So can we repeat this once again: Can we agree that Bosniak children had the right to enroll in Croatian elementary schools without any problem whatsoever in the school year of 1992-1993?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know in that school year, they did have the right to enroll in regular schools.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, to the best of your knowledge, in regular Croatian schools were there any Bosniak children who were enrolled in them in the next school year, from 1993 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were they enrolled without any major problems in these schools, if we do not take into account the objective circumstances as of the capacities of the schools involved?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for those that I gave an affirmative answer to, they enrolled in the previous school year, in 1992-1993, and without any problems they continued in the school year 1993-1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever hear in the school year of 1993-1994 that some children of refugees enrolled in regular elementary schools provisionally and that some children enrolled with the status of guest pupils?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what period I dare speak of. I knew of the status of guest pupils.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. So you knew the status of guest pupils. Tell me, the status of a guest pupil, was it not conceived in order for Bosniak children that had fled to Croatia and that did not have all the necessary documents could continue their regular schooling in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know why it was conceived.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the conditions were for attaining the status of a guest pupil?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you say that a christening certificate was required for enrolling in regular schools, tell me, were christening certificates required for someone to enroll in school as a guest pupil?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, nevertheless, as you worked on these matters, did you not find out that a christening certificate, indeed, could not have been a prerequisite for attaining any kind of status in an elementary school in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have found out about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you have any knowledge to the effect that guest pupils, instead of official diplomas, were issued certificates on a completed grade or year?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you address the Ministry of Education in the second half of 1993 in order to establish the right of pupils to continue their education on the basis of these certificates on having completed a given year or grade?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not dare say whether it was the second half of 1993. But that there were such requests, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I have a document from September 1993. Was it explained that on the basis of these certificates one could continue one's education and that Bosniak children, indeed, normally continued their schooling in the regular Croatian school system?

utterances.speaker: AZRA KRAJSEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
